newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan to reassure Central Asians about Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan to reassure Central Asians about Taleban.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari, keen to allay Central Asian fears about the rise of the radical Islamic Taleban militia in Afghanistan, flies to the Uzbek capital Tashkent on Friday, official sources said.
"The Taleban do not have any territorial ambitions," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Thursday, confirming that Afghanistan would be high on Leghari's Central Asian agenda.
Leghari, due to visit Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan later this month, will discuss trade, transport and communications links, as well as the fast-moving Afghan conflict, the sources said.
Pakistan, which denies charges that it backs the Taleban, has already sent officials to Central Asian states to reassure them about the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban's intentions.

Russia and its former southern republics, alarmed that the Taleban's purist brand of Islam might provoke instability in the region, held a summit in the Kazakh capital Almaty a week after the Sunni Moslem zealots swept into Kabul on September 27.
Delegates vowed to defend areas bordering Afghanistan but pledged not to interfere in the internecine fighting.
Turkmenistan, which has coexisted with Taleban forces holding western Afghan provinces south of its border for more than a year, stayed away from the hastily arranged meeting.
Pakistan is mediating between the Taleban and northern militia chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek, who is widely believed to receive assistance from Uzbekistan.
On Wednesday, Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar brokered the first public, high-level contact between Dostum and the Taleban in the Uzbek leader's northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif.

Further talks were due to take place at Taleban headquarters in the southern city of Kandahar on Thursday, even as witnesses reported that Dostum's forces had actively linked up with those of ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
Dostum sent troops, tanks and artillery into the town of Jabal os-Siraj, north of Kabul, to honour a pledge to join the mainly ethnic Tajik guerrillas led by his former rival Masood.
Before the Taleban conquered Kabul, Pakistan often queried the legitimacy of President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government but now says it will deal with any government holding the capital.

"We continue to favour a broad-based government," the Foreign Ministry spokesman said. "Pakistan will not take sides in an intra-Afghan settlement, which we believe will reflect the prevailing situation in Afghanistan, including ethnicity."

Pakistan supported most of the Islamic guerrilla factions that fought Soviet troops in Afghanistan in the 1980s, but appeared to favour the Taleban, or religious scholars, when they emerged from Islamic colleges in Pakistan in 1994.
In October 1994, Babar despatched a truck convoy aimed at opening up a trade route to Turkmenistan across Afghanistan, but local guerrilla commanders seized the trucks in Kandahar.
The Taleban, then virtually unknown, rescued the convoy, routed the local commanders and swiftly captured Kandahar.
Leghari's tour coincides with plans to send another convoy to Central Asia, this time avoiding Afghanistan.

Twenty trucks carrying rice, wheat and leather goods are due to leave next week from the southern port city of Karachi to Almaty, symbolising Pakistani hopes of building trade ties with potentially oil-rich Central Asian nations.

The convoy's tortuous route -- trundling up the mountainous Karakoram Highway and across the Khunjerab Pass to the Chinese market town of Kashgar and on to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek before winding up in Almaty -- mirrors Pakistan's problems in finding ways to Central Asia that skirt its turbulent neighbour.
Pakistan, China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan agreed in 1994 to encourage trade by improving the 1,285-km (800-mile) highway, completed by Chinese engineers and Pakistani troops in 1978.
Strife in Afghanistan, across which the most direct access routes run, has long foiled Pakistani ambitions to promote Karachi as a port serving landlocked Central Asian countries.
It has also blocked plans to build oil and gas pipelines from Turkmenistan to Pakistan across Afghan soil.
